title: Plan your week: ten minutes on Monday
voice_rule: 4: Group Talent learning piece (recap film for an e-learning)
captions: Monday, 08:52. Tom wants his rigging plan.
Marta wants a lift study by Wednesday.
And the HQ report is due Friday. Nobody’s asked about that one.
Start on whoever calls loudest, and the week lives in your head.
Every call reshuffles it, and the quiet jobs slide later until they’re urgent.
Tom and Marta push for one reason.
They can’t see when their work will come.
So give it ten minutes before you answer. One page.
Every job gets its own date,
and one gets marked as the thing that must happen this week.
Then call Tom back: Tuesday, by noon.
He can plan his crew, and the calls stop.
Dates move. On Tuesday the client’s drawing slips to Thursday.
Before anything goes back in, ask how the last few like it went.
New cost codes, no record yet: extra days.
A permit office that’s been on time six times: trust its date.
A client who only “might” want more: ask first.
Wednesday morning, you open the plan.
The study and the report both need Thursday and Friday.
You see it now, two days early.
Saying so feels like admitting the week went wrong.
Say it anyway, with a proposal.
“Both need Thursday and Friday. I’d do the study first.
Can the report move to Monday?”
Paul answers in one line.
Most weeks get done either way.
What the plan buys you is a calmer one, and Friday’s problem on a Wednesday.
